### A.17 Effect of data scaling

We show the performance of ReMuSE across different scales : 0,10,30 and
100 % in
Fig [14](#A1.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ A.17 Effect of data scaling ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue").
We find that even with smaller training data subsets (10–30%), all the
models achieve substantial gains in K-Precision, Q2-F1, and Specificity,
with Flan-T5 already performing competitively at 10% of the data.
Increasing the training size to 100% provides only modest additional
improvements, suggesting that the algorithmic design and reward-guided
fine-tuning, rather than sheer data scale, drive most of the performance
gains. This highlights that ReMuSE efficiently leverages limited data to
learn knowledge-grounded dialogue behavior.

![Refer to caption](2508.05283v2/images/data_scale.png)

Figure 14: Performance of ReMuSE across different data scales.

### A.18 Dialogue Differences across paper types

We show in
Figure [15](#A1.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ A.21 Operational guidelines for deploying the dialogue agent ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue")
that dialogue length varies across paper types, with borderline papers
exhibiting the longest dialogues (12.2 turns), reflecting the greater
deliberation required for conflicting or ambiguous reviews. Accepted
papers have moderate lengths (8.3 turns), while rejected papers are
shortest (6.1 turns).
Figure [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ A.21 Operational guidelines for deploying the dialogue agent ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue")
shows decision correctness, which is highest for accepted papers (90%)
and slightly lower for rejected (85%), with borderline papers lowest
(78%), indicating that the agent performs best when reviews converge and
faces greater challenges in ambiguous cases. Finally,
Figure [17](#A1.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ A.21 Operational guidelines for deploying the dialogue agent ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue")
presents phase coverage for evidence gathering, conflict resolution, and
consensus formation. Borderline papers have the highest coverage across
all phases, especially conflict resolution (77%), emphasizing structured
deliberation, whereas accepted and rejected papers show slightly lower
coverage. These results highlight that the agent adapts its behavior
according to the complexity of the paper, supporting longer and more
structured dialogues where necessary.

### A.19 Statistical Measures

We find that paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Cohen’s
d, show robust improvements [Cleophas and Zwinderman (2010)](#bib.bib2).
For 15 PhD students, content relevance using the dialogue agent
increased by 0.42 (t(14)=10.84, p$`\leq`$.001, d=3.43) and coverage by
0.52 (t(14)=10.56, p$`\leq`$.001, d=3.34), with task completion time
decreasing by 15 minutes (t(14)=-19.45, p$`\leq`$.001, d=-6.15). In
comparison, Auto Meta-Rev yielded smaller gains (Content Relevance
+0.13, Coverage +0.19). For 10 non-PhD participants, content relevance
rose by 0.54 (t(9)=-13.50, p$`\leq`$.001, d=6.04), coverage by 0.54
(t(9)=-10.59, p$`\leq`$.001, d=4.74), and time decreased by 45 minutes
(t(9)=8.51, p$`\leq`$.001, d=-3.81), while Auto Meta-Rev showed more
modest improvements (Content Relevance +0.22, Coverage +0.25). We do
observe that the very large effect sizes and highly significant p-values
indicate these improvements are likely to generalize to a larger
population, and that the dialogue agent consistently outperforms both
zero-shot and automated meta-review baselines (see
Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5 Deploying Meta-Reviewing Dialogue Agents: A Within-subject Study ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue")).

in comparsion to baselines discussed in
§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Dataset Generation ‣ 3 Synthetic Data Generation for Fine-tuning Meta-review Dialogue Agents ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue")
. Notably, Mixtral’s performance with ReMuSE still surpasses the other
models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the dialogues generated by
our approach.

### A.21 Operational guidelines for deploying the dialogue agent

The following operational guidelines outline measures to prevent misuse
of dialogue agents in systems that implement our approach presented in
Table [16](#A1.T16 "Table 16 ‣ A.21 Operational guidelines for deploying the dialogue agent ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue").

|                                         |                                                 |                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Misuse Prevention Mechanism (Design/UI) | Failure Mode Mitigated                          | Description                                                                                                                                |
| Citation Traceability                   | “Ghostwriting” / Unverified Claims              | UI must display source snippets (reviewer ID, line/context) for all agent-generated claims, enabling instant verification.                 |
| Human Final Decision                    | Automation Bias / Replacement of Human Judgment | The final decision (e.g., “recommend reject”) must be a human-entered field, not an agent-generated output.                                |
| Interleaved Presentation                | Automation Bias / Reduced Critical Reading      | Agent summaries and original source reviews should be presented side-by-side or be easily accessible to encourage comparison.              |
| Balanced Summary View                   | Anchoring Bias                                  | Agent should present arguments for and against the final recommendation with equal prominence (e.g., randomized order).                    |
| Decision Logging                        | Lack of Accountability / Misuse                 | Submission process logs whether the agent was used and which agent-generated arguments were directly adopted, creating an auditable trail. |
| Strict Grounding                        | Confabulation / Hallucination                   | Enforce a hard constraint on generation, penalizing statements not mapped to input text; include a UI warning for any unsourced claims.    |

Table 16: Design/UI mechanisms to mitigate misuse of agent-generated
review feedback.

### A.22 End-to-end Workflow

We present the end-to-end workflow in our paper, summarizing all stages
in
Fig. [18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ A.22 End-to-end Workflow ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Decision-Making with Deliberation:Meta-reviewing as a Document-grounded Dialogue").
First, we generate synthetic dialogues for meta-reviewing using our
proposed method, ReMuSE. Next, we fine-tune dialogue agents to adapt
smaller models for the task of meta-reviewing assistance. Finally, we
deploy the dialogue agent in real-world settings, demonstrating that
this deployment reduces meta-reviewing time by 50%.

#### A.24.1 Meta-Reviewing

The title of the paper is not revealed to retain anonymization. The type
of the paper is “long".

Review 1: Paper is on modeling the prediction of ancestor relation
between names of science institutions. This is on the GRID dataset which
already has some hierarchical information. The proposed approach is
set-based models (with neural encodings) where the overlap between two
names is measured by set overlap at the unigram level. In extended
experiments additional metadata like address and type of institution are
also incorporated into the model (which contribute a lot to the
improvements). A set of simple to intermediate baseline along with
different thresholds of token overlap has been tested and the proposed
model shows strong improvement in the MAP metric. Paper has a decent
writing and structure. Problem and the approach has been explained and
motivated well with descriptive examples. \[…\]

Review 2: The paper shows how to infer the organisational structure of
an institution. That is, it presents a model for predicting the
is-ancestor relationships of institutions based on their string names.
To this end, it makes use of Set-Transformers to model the token overlap
between the institution names. This use is nice but also not highly
original. The experimental evaluation is on a single dataset only. While
the authors do present some examples, and overall hierarchy or something
that provides some more insights into the learned model should be
provided in order to show potential issues with transitivity and
connected components. The evaluation only considers known pairs. But an
organisational structure should also be consistent. That is, the
interesting motivation provided in the intro is not met in the
experimental evaluation. Furthermore, the experimental protocol is
unclear \[…\]

#### A.24.2 Debates

The topic of the paper is: ‘Global Warming is Not a Crisis’. The
arguments for for and against sides of the debate are provided below:

Against side: “Global warming is not a crisis. Please keep in mind what
the proposition is. It is not a debate over whether the earth has been
warming over the past century. Uh, the earth is always warming or
cooling, at least a few tenths of a degree. And we’re talking about, so
far, something on the order of six tenths of a degree centigrade. We’re
not even arguing about whether greenhouse gas emissions are contributing
at some level to warming. And they most certainly should or I would
suggest it would be very little. Indeed, as far as I can tell, even our
opponents do not claim that global warming is a crisis at present.
Rather, we are primarily addressing the future. Now, much of the current
alarm, I would suggest, is based on ignorance of what is normal for
weather and climate. \[…\]

For side: “The motion before us, global warming is not a crisis, means
we ought to know what crisis means. The word does not mean catastrophe
or alarmism. It means a crucial or decisive moment, a turning point, a
state of affairs in which a decisive change for better or worse is
imminent. We are talking about the future here. The entire world now
really does have a critical choice to make. It is whether to continue on
the present path of adding more and more carbon dioxide and other
greenhouse gases to the atmosphere or whether to find another path.
We’re speaking of the future. And science tells us that the path we
choose will largely determine what kind of earth our children and
grandchildren will inherit. Our task tonight is to persuade you that
global warming is indeed a crisis in exactly that precise sense so you
should vote against the motion. The science community today has
impeccable settled science, despite what you have just heard, that
